newsitem.title: USA: Troy, NY says might try to delay $1.4 mln payment.
newsitem.headline: Troy, NY says might try to delay $1.4 mln payment.

text.p: Troy, N.Y., whose finances have been badly battered, is weighing whether to ask some of its bondholders to agree to delay a payment on $35 million of debt that is due Sept 15, city officials said Tuesday.
In the past, rating agencies have regarded late payments as defaults, even if bondholders agree to such delays. But a Troy official said how a possible delay would be viewed is not clear.

Stressing Troy wants to reach an agreement with the three mutual funds that own the bonds, Owen Goldfarb, director of the city's Office of Management and Budget, said "This is not a default. It's just a nonpayment on a lease."

Asked if rating agenices would consider a delay as tantamount to a default, he replied, "We don't really know, that's the whole issue." Goldfarb added Troy hopes to get the bondholders to accept a smaller amount than the $1.4 million that is due in mid-September.

Utica, another upstate New York town whose finances are in bad shape, last month narrowly avoided defaulting on about $25 million of debt as the state comptroller had to step in and buy about $2.145 million of bonds to complete a refinancing.
Whether the state, which included nearly $2.7 million of aid for Troy in its approximately $66 billion budget, will give the city any additional assistance is not yet known.

Goldfarb referred questions on this topic to the comptroller's office, which did not immediately return calls for comment. In late 1994, the comptroller bought the city's bond anticipation notes for its short-term pool until the city could sell its debt publicly.
But since 1995, Troy has been under the control of a state-imposed Municipal Assistance Corp (MAC), which handles the town's debt offerings, as it has been unable to sell debt on its own.
MAC can guarantee bondholders that they will be repaid because it has first rights to state aid and sales tax revenues.

In 1992, Troy's local Industrial Development Agency issued $35 million of debt under a lease back mortgage arrangement, and paid a fairly substantial interest rate of 8.8 percent due to the deal's unusual structure. The mayor said the debt is owned by the Rochester Fund, the Franklin fund and the Van Kampen Fund.

Troy, whose debt service for 1996 in January totaled more than $9 million, or 25 percent of its annual expenses, does not have enough money in its reserve account to make the $1.4 million payment due Sept 15, city officials said.

While saying talks with the bondholders are continuing, Troy mayor Mark Pattison told the town's finance committee last week there were only two alternatives, according to a copy of his prepared remarks. "The holders of the IDA bonds can postpone the September 15 payment pending the completion of the negotiations, or the city may end up in litigation."
But Troy has been able to renegotiate $5 million of debt that was borrowed at a 9.75 percent interest rate in 1990, partly for construction and to buy a professional hockey franchise.
Massachusetts Financial Services, the sole bondholder, agreed to eliminate all future interest payments, so that Troy will only repay the remaining $4.7 million in principal.

The repayment plan calls for restructuring the repayments into a new bond to be sold on the open market, cutting the principal to $2.8 million and the interest to 6.25 percent. The city promised to repay the total $4.7 million by 2010.

And the mayor recommended to the finance committee that the $17 million of short-term notes that now are owned by the state comptroller be converted to long-term bonds that would be issued by the MAC. This would save the city about $500,000 a year in annual debt service.
